## Advanced decision and composition solutions

The solutions below keep the mechanistic simulator visible. Numerical values
are recomputed by the Julia code rather than copied from a previous run.

### Surrogate and emulator models

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-a07-ex1}

Use tuples as the two-dimensional design points. `Surrogates.sample` returns
Latin-hypercube points in the requested rectangle, and the current
`RadialBasis` API accepts those tuples directly.

```{julia}
using CairoMakie, EpiModelingCourse, OrdinaryDiffEq
using Random, Statistics, Surrogates

function a07_q(β, γ)
    p = SIRParameters(beta=β, contact_rate=10.0, gamma=γ, N=1000.0)
    sol = solve(ODEProblem(EpiModelingCourse.sir_ode!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, 40.0), p),
                Tsit5(); saveat=[40.0], abstol=1e-9, reltol=1e-9)
    sol[3, end] / p.N
end

Random.seed!(20260711)
lo, hi = [0.02, 0.15], [0.08, 0.35]
design = Surrogates.sample(24, lo, hi, LatinHypercubeSample())
responses = [a07_q(x[1], x[2]) for x in design]
emulator = RadialBasis(design, responses, lo, hi; rad=cubicRadial())

grid = [(β, γ) for β in range(lo[1], hi[1]; length=5)
                 for γ in range(lo[2], hi[2]; length=5)]
truth = [a07_q(x[1], x[2]) for x in grid]
prediction = emulator.(grid)
errors = prediction .- truth
summary = (rmse=sqrt(mean(errors.^2)),
           max_abs_error=maximum(abs.(errors)),
           training_points=length(design))
@assert all(isfinite, errors)
summary
```

The grid separates validation from the 24 training points. The largest error
identifies a region where the response surface changes most rapidly or where
the design is sparse. Increasing the design or adding targeted points should
be preferred to extrapolating outside the rectangle.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-a07-ex2}

The same two-input design can fit both a terminal recovered fraction and an
internal maximum. The latter is harder because a small parameter change can
move the time of the maximum between output samples.

```{julia}
using CairoMakie, EpiModelingCourse, OrdinaryDiffEq
using Random, Statistics, Surrogates

function a07_peak(β, γ)
    p = SIRParameters(beta=β, contact_rate=10.0, gamma=γ, N=1000.0)
    sol = solve(ODEProblem(EpiModelingCourse.sir_ode!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, 40.0), p),
                Tsit5(); saveat=0.25, abstol=1e-9, reltol=1e-9)
    maximum(sol[2, :]) / p.N
end
function a07_terminal(β, γ)
    p = SIRParameters(beta=β, contact_rate=10.0, gamma=γ, N=1000.0)
    sol = solve(ODEProblem(EpiModelingCourse.sir_ode!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, 40.0), p),
                Tsit5(); saveat=[40.0], abstol=1e-9, reltol=1e-9)
    sol[3, end] / p.N
end

Random.seed!(20260712)
lo, hi = [0.02, 0.15], [0.08, 0.35]
design = Surrogates.sample(24, lo, hi, LatinHypercubeSample())
peak_fit = RadialBasis(design, [a07_peak(x...) for x in design], lo, hi;
                       rad=cubicRadial())
terminal_fit = RadialBasis(design, [a07_terminal(x...) for x in design], lo, hi;
                           rad=cubicRadial())
grid = [(β, γ) for β in range(lo[1], hi[1]; length=5)
                 for γ in range(lo[2], hi[2]; length=5)]
peak_error = peak_fit.(grid) .- [a07_peak(x...) for x in grid]
terminal_error = terminal_fit.(grid) .- [a07_terminal(x...) for x in grid]

fig = Figure(size=(800, 350))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel="validation point", ylabel="absolute error")
scatter!(ax, eachindex(grid), abs.(terminal_error), label="R(40)/N")
scatter!(ax, eachindex(grid), abs.(peak_error), label="max(I)/N")
axislegend(ax)
fig
```

Compare the two error arrays rather than assuming that the peak target is
always worse. The maximum operator is continuous for a well-resolved smooth
trajectory, but it is less smooth as a function of parameters and its
accuracy also depends on the output time grid. That is why an emulator for
peak prevalence needs a denser design and an explicit time-resolution check.

### Model composition and structured populations

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-a08-ex1}

Add a third group and keep total population at 1000. The ODE and jump solves
use the same Catalyst reaction system, so conservation is a stoichiometric
check rather than an assumption added after simulation.

```{julia}
using Catalyst, JumpProcesses, OrdinaryDiffEq, Random

three_group = @reaction_network begin
    @parameters N
    (β*c1)/N, S1 + I1 --> 2I1
    (β*c1*m12)/N, S1 + I2 --> I1 + I2
    (β*c1*m13)/N, S1 + I3 --> I1 + I3
    (β*c2*m21)/N, S2 + I1 --> I2 + I1
    (β*c2)/N, S2 + I2 --> 2I2
    (β*c2*m23)/N, S2 + I3 --> I2 + I3
    (β*c3*m31)/N, S3 + I1 --> I3 + I1
    (β*c3*m32)/N, S3 + I2 --> I3 + I2
    (β*c3)/N, S3 + I3 --> 2I3
    γ, I1 --> R1
    γ, I2 --> R2
    γ, I3 --> R3
end
u0 = [:S1=>330.0,:I1=>3.0,:R1=>0.0,
      :S2=>330.0,:I2=>3.0,:R2=>0.0,
      :S3=>331.0,:I3=>3.0,:R3=>0.0]
p = [:N=>1000.0,:β=>0.05,:c1=>10.0,:c2=>10.0,:c3=>8.0,
     :m12=>0.5,:m21=>0.5,:m13=>0.3,:m31=>0.4,
     :m23=>0.6,:m32=>0.5,:γ=>0.25]
tspan = (0.0, 2.0)
ode = solve(ODEProblem(three_group,u0,tspan,p), Tsit5(); saveat=0.1)
Random.seed!(20260713)
jump = solve(JumpProblem(three_group,
    [pair[1]=>round(Int,pair[2]) for pair in u0], tspan,
    p); saveat=0.1)
function total_population(sol)
    sum(sol[name] for name in (:S1,:I1,:R1,:S2,:I2,:R2,:S3,:I3,:R3))
end
ode_error = maximum(abs.(total_population(ode) .- 1000.0))
jump_error = maximum(abs.(total_population(jump) .- 1000))
@assert ode_error < 1e-7
@assert jump_error == 0
(ode_error=ode_error, jump_error=jump_error,
 aggregate_incidence=1000.0-ode[:S1][end]-ode[:S2][end]-ode[:S3][end])
```

The aggregate curve cannot generally identify all six cross-group multipliers,
especially if only total incidence is observed. Group-specific observations
or informative contact data are needed to distinguish the contact rates and
mixing factors.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-a08-ex2}

Run 100 seeded jump realizations, summarize each time point by a central
interval, and compare the ensemble mean with the deterministic ODE.

```{julia}
using Catalyst, JumpProcesses, OrdinaryDiffEq, Random, Statistics

two_group = @reaction_network begin
    @parameters N
    (β*c1)/N, S1 + I1 --> 2I1
    (β*c1*m12)/N, S1 + I2 --> I1 + I2
    (β*c2*m21)/N, S2 + I1 --> I2 + I1
    (β*c2)/N, S2 + I2 --> 2I2
    γ, I1 --> R1
    γ, I2 --> R2
end
u0 = [:S1=>495,:I1=>5,:R1=>0,:S2=>495,:I2=>5,:R2=>0]
p = [:N=>1000.0,:β=>0.05,:c1=>10.0,:c2=>10.0,
     :m12=>0.5,:m21=>0.5,:γ=>0.25]
times = collect(0.0:0.1:2.0)
ode = solve(ODEProblem(two_group,u0,(0.0,2.0),p), Tsit5(); saveat=times)

trajectories = Matrix{Float64}(undef, length(times), 100)
for replicate in axes(trajectories, 2)
    Random.seed!(20260700 + replicate)
    sol = solve(JumpProblem(two_group,u0,(0.0,2.0),p); saveat=times)(times)
    trajectories[:, replicate] = sol[:I1] .+ sol[:I2]
end
mean_infected = vec(mean(trajectories; dims=2))
lower = [quantile(trajectories[i, :], 0.05) for i in axes(trajectories, 1)]
upper = [quantile(trajectories[i, :], 0.95) for i in axes(trajectories, 1)]

fig = Figure(size=(800,350))
ax = Axis(fig[1,1], xlabel="time", ylabel="aggregate infectious")
band!(ax, times, lower, upper; color=(:steelblue, 0.25))
lines!(ax, times, mean_infected; label="jump mean", color=:steelblue)
lines!(ax, times, ode[:I1] .+ ode[:I2]; label="ODE", color=:black)
axislegend(ax)
fig
```

The band is a pointwise 90% interval, not a simultaneous confidence band.
Increasing `N` makes the diffusion approximation relatively more plausible,
while small counts make discreteness and extinction important. The SDE is a
Gaussian approximation and need not remain inside the jump interval or remain
nonnegative without additional modeling choices.

### Symbolic equilibrium and stability analysis

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-a09-ex1}

The latent class enlarges the infected subsystem from one dimension to two, so
the threshold now comes from a quadratic rather than a single eigenvalue.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-a09-ex1
using Symbolics

# Several loaded packages export `@variables` (Symbolics, Catalyst,
# ModelingToolkitBase, JuMP, InfiniteOpt), so it must be qualified here.
Symbolics.@variables S E I R λ
Symbolics.@variables βc γ μ σ N

seir = [μ*N - βc*S*I/N - μ*S,
        βc*S*I/N - (σ + μ)*E,
        σ*E - (γ + μ)*I,
        γ*I - μ*R]

# The infected subsystem is (E, I); evaluate its Jacobian at the disease-free state.
J_infected = Symbolics.simplify.(Symbolics.substitute.(
    Symbolics.jacobian(seir[2:3], [E, I]), (Dict(S => N, E => 0, I => 0),)))
J_infected
```

```{julia}
#| label: sol-a09-ex1-charpoly
# For a 2x2 matrix the characteristic polynomial is λ² - tr(J)λ + det(J),
# so the Routh--Hurwitz coefficients are available without extracting them.
a₁ = Symbolics.simplify(-(J_infected[1, 1] + J_infected[2, 2]); expand = true)
a₂ = Symbolics.simplify(
    J_infected[1, 1]*J_infected[2, 2] - J_infected[1, 2]*J_infected[2, 1]; expand = true)
(a₁ = a₁, a₂ = a₂)
```

The polynomial is $\lambda^2 + a_1\lambda + a_2$ with
$a_1 = (\sigma+\mu)+(\gamma+\mu)$ and
$a_2 = (\sigma+\mu)(\gamma+\mu) - \beta c\,\sigma$. Routh--Hurwitz for a
quadratic, @eq-a10-rh-quadratic, requires both positive. Since all rates are
positive, $a_1 > 0$ always, so stability turns entirely on $a_2 > 0$:

$$
(\sigma+\mu)(\gamma+\mu) > \beta c\,\sigma
\iff
R_0 = \frac{\beta c\,\sigma}{(\sigma+\mu)(\gamma+\mu)} < 1 .
$$

```{julia}
#| label: sol-a09-ex1-check
R₀_seir = βc*σ/((σ + μ)*(γ + μ))
values = Dict(βc => 0.5, γ => 0.25, μ => 0.01, σ => 0.5, N => 1000.0)
ev(x) = Float64(Symbolics.value(Symbolics.substitute(x, values)))
(R₀ = round(ev(R₀_seir); digits = 4),
 a₂_sign_matches = (ev(a₂) > 0) == (ev(R₀_seir) < 1))
```

**Interpreting $\sigma/(\sigma+\mu)$.** An individual leaves $E$ either by
becoming infectious, at rate $\sigma$, or by dying, at rate $\mu$. The fraction
that survives the latent period is therefore $\sigma/(\sigma+\mu)$. So the SEIR
reproduction number is the SIR one, $\beta c/(\gamma+\mu)$, discounted by the
probability of surviving latency. A long latent period is protective at the
population level when mortality is non-negligible — the exposed individual may
die before ever infecting anyone.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-a09-ex2}

Waning immunity replaces demography, so the population is closed and
$R = N - S - I$ eliminates the third equation.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-a09-ex2
Symbolics.@variables ω
sirs = [-βc*S*I/N + ω*(N - S - I),
        βc*S*I/N - γ*I]

S_star = γ*N/βc
I_star = ω*N*(βc - γ)/(βc*(γ + ω))
residual = Symbolics.simplify.(
    Symbolics.substitute.(sirs, (Dict(S => S_star, I => I_star),)); expand = true)
residual
```

Both residuals vanish identically, so @eq-a10-endemic's analogue for SIRS is
confirmed: $S^\star = \gamma N/\beta c$ and
$I^\star = \omega N(\beta c-\gamma)/(\beta c(\gamma+\omega))$, positive exactly
when $R_0 = \beta c/\gamma > 1$.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-a09-ex2-stability
J_sirs = Symbolics.simplify.(Symbolics.substitute.(
    Symbolics.jacobian(sirs, [S, I]), (Dict(S => S_star, I => I_star),)); expand = true)
trace_sirs = Symbolics.simplify(J_sirs[1, 1] + J_sirs[2, 2]; expand = true)
det_sirs = Symbolics.simplify(
    J_sirs[1, 1]*J_sirs[2, 2] - J_sirs[1, 2]*J_sirs[2, 1]; expand = true)
discriminant = Symbolics.simplify(trace_sirs^2 - 4*det_sirs; expand = true)
(trace = trace_sirs, determinant = det_sirs)
```

The trace is negative and the determinant positive whenever $\beta c > \gamma$,
so the endemic equilibrium is stable throughout its range of existence. The
*character* of the approach is decided by the discriminant
$\operatorname{tr}^2 - 4\det$: negative means complex eigenvalues and a damped
oscillation, positive means a monotone approach.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-a09-ex2-simulate
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using CairoMakie
using LinearAlgebra

function sirs!(du, u, p, t)
    βc_, γ_, ω_, N_ = p
    du[1] = -βc_*u[1]*u[2]/N_ + ω_*(N_ - u[1] - u[2])
    du[2] = βc_*u[1]*u[2]/N_ - γ_*u[2]
end

function classify(ω_value)
    vals = Dict(βc => 0.5, γ => 0.25, ω => ω_value, N => 1000.0)
    e(x) = Float64(Symbolics.value(Symbolics.substitute(x, vals)))
    solution = solve(ODEProblem(sirs!, [990.0, 10.0], (0.0, 400.0),
                                (0.5, 0.25, ω_value, 1000.0)),
                     Tsit5(); saveat = 0.5)
    return (ω = ω_value, discriminant = e(discriminant),
            oscillatory = e(discriminant) < 0, solution = solution)
end

# Find where the discriminant changes sign rather than guessing values.
ω_grid = 0.01:0.01:2.0
discriminants = [Float64(Symbolics.value(Symbolics.substitute(
    discriminant, Dict(βc => 0.5, γ => 0.25, ω => value, N => 1000.0)))) for value in ω_grid]
boundary = ω_grid[findfirst(>(0), discriminants)]

oscillatory_case = classify(boundary / 4)
monotone_case = classify(boundary * 2)
(boundary_ω = round(boundary; digits = 3),
 mean_immune_days_at_boundary = round(1 / boundary; digits = 2),
 oscillatory = (ω = oscillatory_case.ω,
                discriminant = round(oscillatory_case.discriminant; digits = 6),
                is_oscillatory = oscillatory_case.oscillatory),
 monotone = (ω = monotone_case.ω,
             discriminant = round(monotone_case.discriminant; digits = 6),
             is_oscillatory = monotone_case.oscillatory))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-sol-a09-ex2
#| fig-cap: "Approach to the SIRS endemic equilibrium either side of the discriminant condition. Slow waning gives complex eigenvalues and damped oscillations; fast waning gives a monotone approach."
figure = Figure(size = (760, 360))
axis = Axis(figure[1, 1], xlabel = "Time", ylabel = "Infectious")
lines!(axis, oscillatory_case.solution.t, [u[2] for u in oscillatory_case.solution.u];
       color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2,
       label = "ω = $(round(oscillatory_case.ω; digits = 3)) (oscillatory)")
lines!(axis, monotone_case.solution.t, [u[2] for u in monotone_case.solution.u];
       color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2,
       label = "ω = $(round(monotone_case.ω; digits = 3)) (monotone)")
axislegend(axis; position = :rt, framevisible = false)
figure
```

The simulations confirm the symbolic prediction on either side of the boundary.
The epidemiological reading is the interesting part: the sign change happens only
at a very large waning rate, corresponding to immunity lasting on the order of a
single day. For any realistic duration of immunity the discriminant is negative,
so the approach to endemicity is *oscillatory* — the overshoot-and-return cycle
familiar from childhood infections. A monotone approach requires immunity to wane
so fast that the susceptible pool is replenished as quickly as it is depleted,
which is a mathematical regime rather than an epidemiological one.
